correctness.rationale: For each first letter the proof bounds the three disjoint classes by t, \(q-t\) and \((q-1)^2\), hence at most \(q^2-q+1\) and altogether \(q^3-q^2+q\). The idempotent Latin-square code has exactly that cardinality, and disjointness follows from Latin row/column injections plus the diagonal identity. The \(q=2\) case is checked by its explicit six-word set. Published Latin-square existence for every order >=3 supplies the only imported fact, supported by explicit finite examples. Python directly checks \(q=2\),...,6; independent C++ checks odd \(q=3,...,11\). No finite observation is used for the universal proof.

originality.rationale: Full inspection of Sharov–Roth 2014 confirms an arbitrary-alphabet channel and rate bounds, with finite equality discussion focused on binary codes; it does not state or imply exact M_q(4,1) for every q. Gabrys et al. provide binary grain bounds and constructions, while the pre-existing idempotent Latin-square lemma alone cannot establish the grain-optimality statement. Actual claim/alias searches in mathematical records and web did not find the exact general formula. Residual risk: an earlier unindexed q-ary specialization may exist.
residual_risks: An earlier unindexed specialized q-ary length-four enumeration or a subsidiary result not located by the searches could imply the formula.
The complete body of the Kashyap–Zémor binary upper-bound paper was not inspected; its stated binary alphabet focus makes direct all-q coverage unlikely.
The existence of idempotent Latin squares for every q except two is imported from classical design theory; the supplied finite code tests are not a proof of this separate standard existence theorem.

value.rationale: This determines an exact natural coding capacity for every finite alphabet at a first nontrivial overwrite channel length. It couples a sharp symbol-projection counting bound to a universal combinatorial construction, rather than simply recounting a known binary case. The formula reveals an idempotent-Latin-square design principle applicable beyond prime-power alphabets, which is not a mere normalization change or isolated small table.
